1.en: Reconnect the piezo buzzer, then start the program: HALT – NEXT – 00 – RUN.

2.en: The display stays dark for 2 to 3 seconds. The computer is working, as can be seen from the blinking Carry and Zero flags. The display then shows: 00.

3.en: Meanwhile the computer has — invisibly to us — distributed the 4 ships across the playing field. The distribution is made using the random-number generator. The ships are therefore hidden in a different arrangement in every game. Let us assume that the ships are located at the positions marked with crosses on the playing plan (see fig.).

4.en: We can enter two digits. The first digit applies only to the vertical playing-field numbers, the second digit to the horizontal playing-field numbers. As an example we enter 42. The computer responds with a short tone and shows 42. In our example this shot was not a hit.

5.en: If we were now to enter, for example, 15, the computer produces an interval tone and the display reports: AA15. The first ship has been sunk. If we then entered the same number combination once more, no hit would be reported at this point, because the ship has already been sunk.

6.en: As soon as the fourth ship has also been hit, the computer reports back with the interval tone and 3 digits are shown on the display. We can read off how many attempts were needed to hit all 4 ships.

7.en: After pressing any number key, 4 ships are hidden again, the display shows 00 once more, and a new game can begin.

8.en: This is of interest to the programmer:

9.en: We compare the description with the program flow chart and the program table.

10.en: The game is relatively easy to program, because there is no special winning strategy. First the ships must be distributed. Random numbers between 1 and 5 are stored in registers 0 to 7. The coordinates of the first ship are in registers 0 and 1, those of the second ship in registers 2 and 3, and so on.

11.en: By means of the subroutines designated V1 (V = COMPARE), V2 and V3, it is ensured that no square is occupied twice when the ships are distributed.

12.en: The entered coordinates are then stored in registers 8 and 9. Comparison commands are used to check whether the entered coordinates match the coordinates of a hidden ship.

13.en: By means of the subroutine RND a random number is stored in registers D, E and F. The random numbers in registers D and E yield the coordinates of the hidden ships, which is why only the numbers between 1 and 5 are usable. Comparisons are used to check whether a random number of 0 or greater than 5 appears in these registers. If „yes“, the value 9 is added to register D (or the value 3 to register E) for as long as it takes until both random numbers have values between 1 and 5.
